interactions.label: A 60-year-old woman on amlodipine 10 mg for hypertension develops bilateral ankl

params.question: A 60-year-old woman on amlodipine 10 mg for hypertension develops bilateral ankle swelling. Urinalysis and serum albumin are normal. What is the most likely explanation?

answers.text: Congestive heart failure requiring diuretic therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Amlodipine-induced oedema is caused by precapillary arteriolar dilatation, not fluid overload. Diuretics do not resolve this type of swelling.

answers.text: Dose-dependent precapillary vasodilation causing dependent oedema

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Dihydropyridine CCBs dilate arterioles more than venules, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure. This dose-dependent effect occurs in up to 40% of patients at high doses.

answers.text: Nephrotic syndrome from drug-induced renal injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Normal albumin and urinalysis exclude nephrotic syndrome. Amlodipine does not cause significant renal injury.

answers.text: Allergic angioedema requiring immediate drug withdrawal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Angioedema typically involves the face and airway, not dependent ankle swelling. Amlodipine oedema is a pharmacological effect, not an allergic reaction.

overallFeedback.feedback: The oedema is dose-related, caused by dihydropyridine-induced arteriolar vasodilation that raises capillary hydrostatic pressure. It affects up to 40% of patients at high doses and does not respond to diuretics.
Exactly right. Amlodipine causes dose-dependent peripheral oedema through precapillary vasodilation — this is why diuretics do not help.

interactions.label: Aliskiren can be safely combined with an ACE inhibitor to achieve more complete

params.question: Aliskiren can be safely combined with an ACE inhibitor to achieve more complete blockade of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This combination is actually contraindicated. Trials showed that dual RAAS blockade with aliskiren plus an ACE inhibitor or ARB raised the risk of kidney failure and dangerously high potassium without added clinical benefit.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done. Clinical trials demonstrated that combining aliskiren with an ACE inhibitor or ARB significantly increased the risk of renal failure and hyperkalaemia. This combination is now contraindicated.

params.question: How does the effect of thiazide diuretics on calcium handling differ from that of loop diuretics?

answers.text: Both classes cause calcium loss, but thiazides cause less

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The difference is qualitative, not merely quantitative. Thiazides actually promote calcium retention, while loop diuretics promote calcium loss — opposite effects with distinct clinical applications.

answers.text: Thiazides promote calcium retention whereas loop diuretics promote calcium loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Thiazides enhance calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule, reducing urinary calcium — making them useful in recurrent calcium stone disease. Loop diuretics inhibit calcium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, causing hypocalcaemia.

answers.text: Loop diuretics retain calcium, which is why they are used to prevent osteoporosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: It is the opposite. Loop diuretics cause calcium loss (hypocalcaemia). Thiazides retain calcium and are sometimes preferred when calcium conservation is desirable.

answers.text: Neither class significantly affects calcium levels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both classes have clinically significant and opposite effects on calcium. This distinction is high-yield: thiazides retain calcium (useful in stone disease), while loop diuretics waste calcium (risk of hypocalcaemia).

overallFeedback.feedback: Thiazides promote calcium retention (useful in calcium stone disease), while loop diuretics cause calcium loss. This opposite effect on calcium handling is determined by their different sites of action along the nephron.
Correct. This calcium-handling difference is clinically important: thiazides are preferred in calcium stone disease, while loop diuretics can cause hypocalcaemia.

params.question: In a patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and sinus rhythm, digoxin is added to optimal quadruple therapy. What outcome should the patient expect?

answers.text: Reduced mortality similar to ACE inhibitors

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Digoxin does NOT reduce mortality in sinus rhythm. Unlike the four mortality-reducing pillars (ACEi/ARNI, specific beta-blockers, MRAs, SGLT2 inhibitors), digoxin is purely a symptom-management drug.

answers.text: Reduced hospitalisations but no improvement in survival

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The DIG trial showed that digoxin reduces heart failure hospitalisations and improves symptoms but has no effect on mortality in sinus rhythm. Its narrow therapeutic index also demands careful monitoring.

answers.text: Improved survival only if combined with an SGLT2 inhibitor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Digoxin does not improve survival regardless of combination. SGLT2 inhibitors independently reduce mortality and are one of the four mortality-reducing pillars — their benefit is not linked to digoxin.

answers.text: No clinical benefit whatsoever; the drug should be avoided

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Digoxin does have a role: it reduces hospitalisations and improves symptoms. The crucial distinction is that it does not reduce mortality, unlike the four pillars of HFrEF therapy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Digoxin reduces hospitalisations but does NOT improve survival in sinus rhythm. The four pillars that DO reduce mortality are: ACEi/ARNI, specific beta-blockers (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate), MRAs, and SGLT2 inhibitors.
Well answered. Digoxin improves symptoms and reduces hospitalisations but does not reduce mortality — a crucial distinction from the four mortality-reducing HF drug pillars.

interactions.label: What property makes amiodarone pharmacologically unique among the antiarrhythmic

params.question: What property makes amiodarone pharmacologically unique among the antiarrhythmic drugs?

answers.text: It is the only antiarrhythmic available in both oral and intravenous forms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Several antiarrhythmics have dual formulations. Amiodarone's uniqueness lies in its mechanism of action: it simultaneously blocks ion channels across all four Vaughan-Williams classes.

answers.text: It acts on ion channels corresponding to all four Vaughan-Williams classes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Amiodarone blocks sodium channels (Class I), has antisympathetic properties (Class II), blocks potassium channels (Class III — its primary classification), and blocks calcium channels (Class IV). This broad action explains both its efficacy and its complex side-effect profile.

answers.text: It selectively blocks the funny current in sinoatrial node pacemaker cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blocking the funny current (If) is the mechanism of ivabradine, not amiodarone. Amiodarone's primary classification is as a Class III potassium channel blocker, but it acts across all four classes.

answers.text: It is the only antiarrhythmic that does not prolong the QT interval

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Amiodarone DOES prolong the QT interval through its Class III potassium channel blockade. Despite this, torsades de pointes is relatively rare with amiodarone compared to other QT-prolonging drugs.

overallFeedback.feedback: Amiodarone is unique because it acts on all four Vaughan-Williams classes simultaneously: sodium channel blockade (I), antisympathetic effects (II), potassium channel blockade (III), and calcium channel blockade (IV).
Exactly right. Amiodarone acts across all four Vaughan-Williams classes — Na⁺, K⁺, and Ca²⁺ channel blockade plus antisympathetic activity — making it the broadest-spectrum antiarrhythmic available.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old man with known Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome presents with an irr

params.question: A 30-year-old man with known Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome presents with an irregularly irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 220 bpm. Which of the following is a safe treatment option?

answers.text: Intravenous verapamil

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Verapamil blocks the AV node but leaves the accessory pathway unaffected. In WPW with AF, this forces all fibrillatory impulses through the accessory pathway at rates up to 250–350 bpm, risking ventricular fibrillation.

answers.text: Intravenous adenosine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adenosine transiently blocks the AV node but has no effect on the accessory pathway. In WPW with AF, this can precipitate ventricular fibrillation by removing the competing slower pathway.

answers.text: Oral digoxin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Digoxin slows AV nodal conduction but does not block the accessory pathway. Like verapamil and adenosine, it can cause lethal ventricular rates in WPW with atrial fibrillation.

answers.text: Intravenous amiodarone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Amiodarone prolongs refractoriness in both the AV node AND the accessory pathway, making it safe in WPW with AF. Procainamide and immediate DC cardioversion are also acceptable options.

overallFeedback.feedback: In WPW with AF, avoid all pure AV node blockers — verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, and adenosine leave the accessory pathway wide open, risking ventricular fibrillation. Safe options are amiodarone, procainamide, or DC cardioversion.
Correct. In WPW with AF, all pure AV node blockers (verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, adenosine) are contraindicated. Amiodarone, procainamide, or DC cardioversion are the safe choices.
